newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Cargill said eyeing North Korea's rich minerals.
newsitem.headline: Cargill said eyeing North Korea's rich minerals.

text.p: By bartering wheat for zinc with North Korea, U.S. grains giant Cargill Inc is eyeing long-term prospects in an impoverished land that is nevertheless rich in metals, including gold, traders said on Wednesday.

Industry analysts in Seoul said Cargill's hard-fought deal was worth little to the company immediately. But they speculated Cargill may have a longer-term strategy, anticipating an eventual easing of the U.S. trade embargo with the communist North.

North Korea's mineral deposits are plentiful but it has no hard currency to keep its mines and processing plants working. It may welcome foreign investment in a key industrial area, the analysts said.

The country has zinc smelters and refiners near the west coast port of Nampo and in the east coast port of Hungnam, said a manager at Daewoo Corp, South Korea's largest metals trader which does brisk barter business with the North.
"Facilities near Nampo are old and need to be rebuilt, while those near Hungnam have delivery problems. In winter, logistics are very bad in North Korea," he said.

"We cannot rule out the possibilty that Cargill might want to build a new smelter and refinery for zinc," he said. "North Korea would welcome this since it could secure food and hard currency by offering low labour costs."
So far, Cargill has said only that its agreement with Pyongyang was for the sale of wheat.
Industry sources in Seoul said the U.S. company had reached an accord to swap 20,000 tonnes of wheat worth $4 million for a 4,000-tonne shipment of zinc worth an equivalent amount.
The U.S. government eased its trade ban with North Korea to facilitate the Cargill deal, giving the company permission to sell up to 500,000 tonnes of grain.
Zinc is North Korea's most promising mineral export, said Hong Song-kuk, a director at South Korea's Ministry of National Unification.
Pyongyang has abundant supplies of the metal, and North Korean zinc is listed on the London Metal Exchange.
Last year, South Korea imported 29,400 tonnes of North Korean zinc worth $31 million, compared with 47,800 tonnes in 1995 worth $50 million, according to national unification ministry figures.
However, the biggest mineral import from North Korea in value terms is gold. Gold imports last year totalled 4.7 tonnes worth $58 million, against 6.4 tonnes valued at $78 million a year earlier.
Most South Korean trade with the North is barter.
Inter-Korean trade last year was damaged after Seoul froze all contacts with the North following a submarine incursion in September.
South Korea also buys steel and pig iron from across the border. South Korean metals houses prefer buying from the North because these imports are exempt from a three percent tax.
Magnesite, a rare metal, is now the only commodity North Korea can legally export to the United States, Seoul officials said.
Seoul estimates North Korean magnesite ore deposits at about 6.5 billion tonnes, but there is little global demand for the magnesite because of its poor quality.
South Korea estimates the North's zinc deposits at 12 million tonnes, gold deposits at 1,000 tonnes, iron ore at three billion tonnes and anthracite coal at 11.74 billion tonnes.
The coal is also of a poor quality and cannot be exported.
